newsitem.title: UK: Non-EU central banks may be wary of EMU - banker.
newsitem.headline: Non-EU central banks may be wary of EMU - banker.

text.p: Central banks outside the European Monetary Union (EMU) may be unwilling to sell gold while there is uncertainty over Europe's change to a single currency, a senior bullion bank official said on Tuesday.
Lester Solden, senior vice president and director of central bank and government sector trading at Republic National Bank was speaking at the fifth Central Banking Conference.
"In fact some non European Union countries may be happy to sell European currencies in order to buy gold," he said.
There could be diversification out of European currencies while the new European monetary system stabilises early next century.
Moving out of European currencies presented three options, Solden said -- to move reserves into U.S. dollars, into yen or to diversify into gold.

He noted that over the past decade the gold market had been supply-side driven and in addition about 2,500 tonnes of central bank gold was in the market largely as a result of increased producer hedging programmes.
However current returns for gold miners could be threatened if slowing growth in the gold-affinity Asian economies led to a downturn in demand.
Further, more central banks could mobilise gold reserves.
Sales by the International Monetary Fund, other central banks and concerns over the European Central Bank (ECB) "may not lead to confidence in central institutions", he said.

Helen Junz, former economic director of the World Gold Council, remarked at the same conference that Asian economies had refrained from adding gold to their reserves "because of IMF demonitisation" she said referring to IMF plans to sell gold from its reserve to help the poorest nations.
If the ECB had about 20 percent of its reserves in gold, that would "give a positive signal for holding gold," she said.
The national central banks in Europe having contributed from their reserves to the ECB may start looking for higher income to make up for that loss.
"They may create opportunities in the lending market which had not been there before," she said.
